issues.legal_issue: A claimant who relies on false factual allegations is not entitled to the equitable relief of specific performance, and the discretion to grant that relief must be exercised on sound legal principles.
material_facts: The claimant sought specific performance of an agreement to sell property.

The claimant alleged that possession of a property portion had been delivered under the agreement, but the evidence showed that the portion was delivered to the sellers after the tenant vacated it and was later handed to the purchaser.
The claimant alleged that he had informed the purchaser of the agreement, but did not testify to having done so, and the purchaser denied receiving that information.
The claimant alleged an additional payment that was not pleaded in the plaint.
The lower courts refused specific performance, finding that the claimant had made false allegations.
issues.conclusion: The refusal to grant specific performance was justified because the claimant did not come to court with clean hands; the discretion under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, was exercised on sound legal principles and not arbitrarily.
issues.legal_principle: Specific performance is an equitable relief governed by the court’s discretion under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. That discretion cannot be refused arbitrarily and must be exercised on sound principles of law capable of correction by an appellate court. A party seeking equitable relief must come with clean hands, and a party who makes false allegations is not entitled to specific performance. The Court states that this principle has been repeatedly affirmed, but cites no earlier cases by name.

predicates.specific_performance_claim: The claimant sought a decree requiring performance of an agreement to sell property.
predicates.claimant_made_false_factual_allegations: The claimant made factual allegations about the transaction that the court found false.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks specific performance and makes false factual allegations, the rule requires denial of that relief.

issues.legal_issue: A concurrent finding that a purchaser acquired property for value without notice of an earlier agreement does not warrant interference when it rests on an assessment of the evidence.
material_facts: The trial court and the High Court found that the purchaser had no knowledge of the claimant’s agreement and was a bona fide purchaser for value without notice.
The High Court’s finding was concurrent and followed its assessment of the evidence.
The claimant challenged the refusal of specific performance in a special leave petition.
issues.conclusion: The concurrent finding that the purchaser was a bona fide purchaser for value without notice did not warrant interference, and the refusal of specific performance was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the finding that the purchaser had no notice as a concurrent finding of fact based on appreciation of the evidence and concluded that it did not warrant interference. The judgment cites no provision or earlier case for this point.

predicates.specific_performance_challenge: A party challenged the refusal of a claim for specific performance.
predicates.concurrent_finding_of_purchaser_without_: The lower courts both found, after assessing the evidence, that the purchaser had no notice of the earlier agreement.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance challenge concerns a concurrent evidence-based finding that the purchaser had no notice of the earlier agreement, the rule is not to reopen that finding.
